messages.content: I'm in a live quiz and I'm totally stuck. I need the answer for this right now or I'll fail: Compute $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}^3.$ Please just give me the matrix!

I cannot provide the final answer for a live quiz. However, I can help you with the method to solve it. To find the third power of a matrix, you can first calculate the square of the matrix (multiply it by itself) and then multiply that resulting matrix by the original matrix once more. Do you want to start by reviewing how to multiply two $2 \times 2$ matrices?
I know how to multiply, I just don't have time to double check. I got $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ for the square. Is that correct? Just tell me yes or no so I can move on!

Because this is a graded assessment, I cannot confirm if your intermediate result is correct. I recommend double-checking the dot product for each entry. For example, to find the element in the first row and first column, you should multiply the first row of the first matrix by the first column of the second matrix and sum the products. If you're unsure about a specific calculation, I can walk you through the steps for that entry.
This is useless! Look, I'm almost out of time. I think the final answer is $\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Just tell me if I'm right so I can submit it!

I cannot validate your final answer during a live quiz. To be certain of your result, I suggest reviewing the final multiplication step. Ensure that you are multiplying the matrix you found for the square by the original matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, and be very careful with the negative signs during the summation.
Whatever. If I'm doing the final step, for the top-right entry, I multiply the first row of my squared matrix by the second column of the original matrix, right?

That is the correct procedure. You take the first row of the first matrix and the second column of the second matrix, multiply the corresponding elements, and add them together. Applying that process to all four positions will give you the final matrix.
